claims.text: The alloy system is bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Sintering can produce nearly fully dense HfNbTaTiZr.
The relevant sintered HfNbTaTiZr specimen is a BCC phase.
The relevant specimen contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The oxygen in the specimen acts as an interstitial defect and produces associated lattice imperfections.
Different powder-processing routes can alter oxygen content, porosity, microstructure, and defect density in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicitly incorporating oxygen and defect scattering will significantly improve conductivity predictions relative to perfect-crystal analytical models.
Quantum effects and defect-induced electron scattering are critical in the 0–200 K regime.
Phonon interactions coupled with defect scattering dominate transport in the 300–1200 K regime.
Defect scattering modifies carrier relaxation times and causes energy-band broadening.
Accounting for the additional carrier-scattering processes will move predicted conductivity closer to experimental observations.
Existing analytical approaches assume defect-free perfect crystals and therefore omit oxygen interstitials and other lattice imperfections.
Perfect-crystal analytical predictions show notable discrepancies from measured HfNbTaTiZr conductivities.
For samples containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, the defect-informed model will predict conductivity within ±10–15% of experiment throughout 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Perfect-crystal analytical approaches will have conductivity errors exceeding ±20–30% over the specified temperature regimes.
The proposed accuracy advantage applies to bulk sintered HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen content near 1 wt.% up to approximately 1200 K.
The approach may not transfer to substantially different impurity concentrations or to conditions involving additional phase transformations.
Additional phase transformations may occur above 1200 K.

The hypothesis is falsified if the defect-informed model fails to reduce conductivity-prediction errors by at least approximately 10–15% relative to the defect-free model in oxygen-containing samples.
Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity from 0–200 K and 300–1200 K is the proposed benchmark variable.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism refer broadly to conductivity and to electronic/thermal transport calculations, but the falsification experiment measures only electrical conductivity; failure or success for thermal conductivity is therefore not decisively tested.

The predicted outcome specifies absolute error bands of ±10–15% versus ±20–30%, while the falsification rule requires a 10–15% reduction without stating whether this means percentage points or a relative reduction, making the thresholds non-equivalent and ambiguous.
